rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
What is meant by the Rate law and Rate constant of a reaction. Identify the order of a reaction if the units of its Rate constant are :
(a) \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,L\,s^{-1}}\)
rows.solution:
The RATE LAW is the expression giving the rate of a reaction in terms of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to a power that is determined EXPERIMENTALLY and not read off the balanced equation.

The RATE CONSTANT, \(k\), is the proportionality constant in that expression — equivalently, the rate of the reaction when the molar concentration of every reactant is unity.

The units of \(k\) follow from the order, because the rate itself always carries units of mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\):
(a) \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) means \(k\) = rate divided by one power of concentration, so the reaction is FIRST order.
(b) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\) means \(k\) = rate divided by concentration SQUARED, so the reaction is SECOND order.

The general rule is that \(k\) has units \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\) for order \(n\), which lets the order be read straight off the units.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{8MnO_4^{-}} + \mathrm{3S_2O_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{3Sn^{2+}} + \mathrm{14H^{+}} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) In neutral or faintly alkaline solution permanganate is reduced only as far as manganese dioxide, while thiosulphate is oxidised all the way to sulphate:
\(8\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 3\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 8\mathrm{MnO_2} + 6\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)

The unusual 8 : 3 ratio is worth checking by electrons: manganese goes \(+7\) to \(+4\), three electrons each for eight atoms, twenty-four in all; and in each thiosulphate the two sulphurs go from an average \(+2\) to \(+6\), four electrons each, eight per ion and twenty-four for three ions.

(b) Acidified dichromate oxidises tin(II) to tin(IV) and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 3\mathrm{Sn^{2+}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{Sn^{4+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Here two chromiums take three electrons each and three tins give two each, so six pass either way.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following observations :
(a) p-Chloronitrobenzene reacts with (aq)NaOH at 443 K to give p-nitrophenol whereas chlorobenzene reacts with the same reagent at 623 K and 300 atm.
(b) Main product obtained when chloroethane reacts with KCN is propane nitrile while with Ag CN it is ethyl isocyanide.
rows.solution:
(a) Because of the electron-WITHDRAWING nitro group. Nucleophilic substitution on an aryl halide proceeds through an intermediate carrying a negative charge on the ring, and a nitro group ortho or para to the halogen can take that charge onto its own oxygen atoms by resonance. In p-chloronitrobenzene the nitro group sits para to the chlorine and stabilises the intermediate, so hydroxide attacks at 443 K. Chlorobenzene has no such group: its intermediate is unstabilised, and the reaction needs 623 K and 300 atm to proceed at all.

(b) The cyanide ion is AMBIDENT — it can attack through carbon or through nitrogen — and which end attacks depends on how the reagent holds it. Potassium cyanide is predominantly ionic, so it releases a free cyanide ion; both atoms could donate, but attack through CARBON prevails because the \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond formed is stronger than a \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bond would be, and the product is the alkyl cyanide, propanenitrile. Silver cyanide is mainly covalent, so the carbon is tied up in the bond to silver and only the nitrogen lone pair is free to attack; the product is then the isocyanide, ethyl isocyanide.

rows.stem: Henry's law constant for \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in water is \(1.67 \times 10^{8}\) Pa at 298 K. Calculate the number of moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in 540 g of soda water when packed under \(3.34 \times 10^{5}\) Pa at the same temperature.
rows.solution:
Henry's law in the mole-fraction form gives the amount dissolved:
\(x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{K_H} = \dfrac{3.34 \times 10^{5}}{1.67 \times 10^{8}} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\)

Strictly \(x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} + n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}\), but the solution is very dilute, so the denominator may be taken as \(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}}\) alone. Soda water is essentially water, so 540 g of it gives
\(n_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = \dfrac{540}{18} = 30\ \mathrm{mol}\)

and therefore
\(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 30 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Both pressures are in pascals, so no conversion is needed and the mole fraction comes out dimensionless.

rows.stem:
Give reasons :
(a) Fuel cells are preferred for production of electrical energy than thermal plants.
(b) Iron does not rust even if zinc coating is broken in a galvanized pipe.
(c) In the experimental determination of electrolytic conductance, Direct Current (DC) is not used.
rows.solution:
(a) Two reasons. A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of the fuel DIRECTLY into electrical energy, so it is not limited by the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine and reaches a far higher efficiency — around 70% against the 40% or so of a thermal plant. And it is pollution free: a hydrogen-oxygen cell produces only water, whereas a thermal plant burning fossil fuel releases carbon dioxide and oxides of sulphur and nitrogen.

(b) Because the zinc protects the iron ELECTROCHEMICALLY, not merely physically. Zinc has a more negative electrode potential than iron, so wherever the two are in contact the zinc is oxidised in preference and the iron is not. Breaking the coating exposes bare iron, but that iron is still in contact with zinc, which continues to corrode as a sacrificial anode and keeps the iron cathodic. A coating of tin, whose potential is less negative than iron's, would behave the opposite way and make corrosion worse once scratched.

(c) Because direct current would ELECTROLYSE the solution. A steady current in one direction discharges ions at the electrodes, so the composition of the solution changes while the measurement is being made, and the products collecting on the electrodes polarise them and add an unknown resistance of their own. Alternating current reverses many times a second, so no net electrolysis occurs and nothing accumulates.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(a) \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}/Mn})}\) is \(-1.18\) V. Why is this value highly negative in comparison to neighbouring d-block elements ?
(b) What is lanthanoid contraction ?
(c) Zn, Cd and Hg are soft metals. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is exceptionally stable. Removing two electrons from a manganese atom leaves \(3d^5\), an exactly half-filled subshell with all five spins parallel, which is a particularly favourable arrangement. Since the product of the oxidation is so stable, the metal gives up those two electrons readily, the oxidation is strongly favoured, and the reduction potential is correspondingly more negative than the general trend across the series would suggest.

(b) Lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series from lanthanum to lutetium. Each added electron enters a 4f orbital, and f electrons shield the outer electrons from the nucleus very poorly, so the effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost shell grows steadily and pulls it inwards.

(c) Because their metallic bonding is weak. Zinc, cadmium and mercury all have the configuration \((n-1)d^{10}ns^2\): the d subshell is completely filled and the \(ns\) electrons are paired, so no unpaired electron is available for interatomic bonding. With only weak metallic bonds holding the lattice together, the metals are soft and low-melting — mercury being liquid at room temperature.

rows.stem:
(a) Using valence bond theory, explain the hybridization and magnetic behaviour of the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{K_2[NiCl_4]}\)
[At. no. : Co = 27, Ni = 28]
(b) Write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^{5}}\) ion when \(\Delta_\mathrm{o} > \mathrm{P}\).
rows.solution:
(a)(i) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\). The three chlorides outside make the complex cation \(+3\), and the six ammine ligands are neutral, so cobalt is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a strong field ligand, so it pairs all six electrons into three \(3d\) orbitals, leaving two empty for bonding.
Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\), octahedral; magnetic character: DIAMAGNETIC, since no electron is left unpaired.

(ii) \(\mathrm{K_2[NiCl_4]}\). The two potassium ions make the complex anion \(-2\), and four chlorido ligands contribute \(-4\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), with two unpaired electrons. Chloride is a weak field ligand and cannot force them to pair, so bonding uses the outer \(4s\) and \(4p\) orbitals.
Hybridisation: \(sp^3\), tetrahedral; magnetic character: PARAMAGNETIC, with two unpaired electrons.

Note the contrast with \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\), where the strong field cyanide pairs those two electrons and gives a \(dsp^2\) square planar diamagnetic complex from the same metal ion.

(b) When \(\Delta_0 > \mathrm{P}\) the field is strong, so pairing electrons in the lower set costs less than promoting one to the upper set. A \(d^5\) ion therefore crowds all five electrons into the \(t_{2g}\) orbitals:
\(t_{2g}^5\ e_g^0\)
This is the low spin arrangement, with just one unpaired electron.
